summary: Petrana Radulovic argues that Disney's centennial year, capped by the film Wish, shows a company relying too heavily on nostalgia, remakes and spinoffs. She says this is profitable but unsustainable, and that Disney's true legacy is risk-taking and innovation, as seen in Fantasia, Lilo & Stitch and The Little Mermaid. Nostalgia works best as a side ingredient, not the main offering, if Disney wants to last another century.
one_line: Polygon op-ed argues Disney should stop leaning on nostalgia and remakes and return to the risky innovation that built its century-long legacy.
key_facts: Wish is Walt Disney Animation's newest movie and the culmination of the studio's centennial celebration in 2023.
Disney's centennial included the short Once Upon a Studio, merchandise drops for each decade, and a rebrand of the Disney castle logo.
Disney's live-action remakes and sequels consistently get mixed to poor reviews but still make hundreds of millions of dollars.
After John Lasseter became Disney's chief creative officer in 2006, he canned the direct-to-video sequel department a year later, reportedly because cheap sequels diminished the Disney brand.
Disney announced a live-action version of 2016's animated hit Moana, which the author says hasn't had time to build its own legacy.
The Black Cauldron almost bankrupted the studio in 1985.
The original 1940 Fantasia was a box-office failure, yet the Sorcerer Mickey short is as iconic as Mickey himself.
Lilo & Stitch was hidden by its filmmakers from the rest of the company and made back more than three times its budget.
The Little Mermaid kickstarted the Disney Renaissance and was a risk because a Broadway-style animated musical hadn't been done before.
Walt Disney modeled his theme park entrances after how his hometown looked at the turn of the 20th century, showing he was also nostalgic.
The author argues nostalgia works best on the side, in shorts, parades and merchandise, rather than as the main offering.
The author says fans want different things, and what they really miss is the feeling of discovering something new.
